newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to make more changes in economic team.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to make more changes in economic team.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto will make further changes in her economic team soon, newly-appointed Finance Minister Naveed Qamar said on Thursday.

Minister of State for Finance Makhdoom Shahabuddin would be assigned a new portfolio in the near future and one or two other ministers might be added "within the overall economic team" in the next few days, he told a news conference .
Qamar indicated this would not involve an expansion of the existing cabinet, but gave no details.
Qamar took over the finance portfolio on Monday from Bhutto, who had held it since her government took power in October 1993.
V.A. Jafarey, who effectively ran the ministry as Bhutto's adviser on finance and economic affairs, has gone on leave.
Qamar, 41, has retained his previous post as Privatisation Minister. Moeen Afzal, additional secretary at the finance ministry, was promoted to secretary in place of Mian Tayyeb.
The chairman of the private Muslim Commercial Bank, Hussain Lawai, was named as a consultant to the finance ministry and Qamar said two or three more such advisers might be drafted in.
Critics had argued that Bhutto lacked the expertise to run the finance ministry herself and should appoint a new economic team to try to restore Pakistan's battered international image.
Qamar signalled that he would now take overall charge of economic policy-making. "There shall be only one finance minister," he said, promising a new policy of consultation.
"Our philosophy is now to be more open and open up overall the finance ministry and be more sensitive to the issues of the private sector and of trade, industry and agriculture," he said.
"I think it important that we get more input and that we involve them in the entire process."

Previously several people, including Jafarey, Bhutto's special assistant for the economy Shahid Hasan Khan and State (central) Bank governor Muhammad Yaqub, as well as Bhutto, wielded varying degrees of influence over economic strategy.
